summary: This document extends DLEP with a credit window scheme aware of Diffserv, supporting both destination-specific and shared flow control. It builds on the base DLEP credit window mechanism.

plainLanguage.summary: DLEP is the protocol a router and a modem use to exchange information about the link between them. It has no way to tell the router to slow down when the modem's queues fill up. This document adds that: the modem lists credit windows, and the router matches each outgoing packet to a window using where the packet is going and its Diffserv class before sending it.

subtitle: How a modem tells a router which queue to send to, matched by destination and Diffserv class.

tldr.problem: DLEP exchanges link control information between a router and a modem, but the base specification has no way to slow the router down when the modem's queues fill up.
tldr.mechanism: The document adds the Diffserv Aware Credit Window extension. The modem advertises credit windows, the router classifies each packet by DLEP destination and DSCP to find the matching window, and sends the packet only while that window has credit.
tldr.outcome: Credit windows can be shared across destinations and DSCP values or reserved for one of them, and a router MUST NOT send traffic whose window has no credit. IANA has assigned the extension Extension Type value 6.

facts.label: Credit windows
facts.value: One or more, each typically with a virtual or physical queue

facts.label: Window scope
facts.value: Shared across destinations and DSCPs, or dedicated to one

facts.label: No credit available
facts.value: The router MUST NOT send that traffic to the modem

today: RFC 9894 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026. It adds an extension to the DLEP specification in RFC 8175 and depends on the traffic classification and credit window documents RFC 9892 and RFC 9893, which were published at the same time.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP), defined in RFC 8175, lets two peers exchange control information about a link. A DLEP session runs between a modem and a router. DLEP defines a base set of mechanisms and a way to add extensions, and this document defines one such extension.

The base DLEP specification includes no flow control at all, and that is the gap this document fills. The extension provides flow control for the traffic a router sends to a modem, using one or more logical credit windows. Each window is typically supported by an associated virtual or physical queue. A credit is permission to send: the router uses the traffic classification information supplied by the modem to work out which window a packet belongs to, and sends that packet only while the window has credits left.

The mechanism reuses the traffic classification and credit window flow control mechanisms defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893, and adds the Diffserv dimension on top. The result is called the Diffserv Aware Credit Window extension, or more simply the DA Credit extension. Where both Diffserv and Ethernet traffic classification are specified for a flow, as in Section 2.3.1 of RFC 9892, the Ethernet information takes precedence.
sections.plainLanguage: DLEP is how a router and a modem exchange link information. It has no built-in way to slow the router down when the modem's queues fill. This document adds credit windows: the modem lists them, and the router checks that the window a packet belongs to still has credit before sending it.

sections.title: Extension Usage and Identification
sections.content:
An implementation signals that it uses the extension by including the Diffserv Aware Credit Window Extension Type value in the Extensions Supported Data Item, which is described in Section 13.6 of RFC 8175. That data item is sent and processed according to RFC 8175.

Support is all or nothing in a specific sense. An implementation that indicates use of the Diffserv Aware Credit Window extension MUST support all message types, data items, the Diffserv Traffic Classification Sub-Data Item and all related processing defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893. The Extension Type value assigned to the extension is 6.
sections.plainLanguage: A router and a modem say they support the extension by listing it in the data item that carries supported extensions. Once listed, the implementation has to handle everything the two supporting documents define, not just the Diffserv matching.

sections.title: Management Considerations
sections.content:
Support for the extension MUST be declared using the Extensions Supported Data Item, and Diffserv Aware Credit Window data items MUST NOT be emitted by a DLEP participant unless that support was specified in the initialization message received from its peer. The use of the extension SHOULD be configurable on both modems and routers. That configuration can be implemented with a proprietary command-line interface or by implementing a YANG module, whose definition is out of scope for this document.

On the modem side, the document says modems SHOULD support configuring the mapping of a DSCP to a credit window, that is, to a queue. Modems MAY support configuring the number of credit windows to advertise to a router.

Routers have limits of their own. A router may support only a few queues, may not support per-destination queues at all, and may not support every combination of credit windows. When the credit window information a modem provides exceeds the capabilities of a router, the router SHOULD use a subset of the provided credit windows. Alternatively, a router MAY reset the session and indicate that the extension is not supported. In either case, any mismatch in capabilities SHOULD be reported to the user through normal network management mechanisms, such as user interface messages or error logging.

One rule holds in all cases: while credit windows are in use, traffic for which credits are not available MUST NOT be sent to the modem by the router.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends should let an operator turn the feature on or off, and a modem should let an operator map each Diffserv class to a queue. If a modem advertises more windows than a router can handle, the router uses the ones it can and tells the operator about the mismatch. The rule that never bends: a router does not send traffic that has no credit left.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension uses DLEP mechanisms and the credit window flow control mechanisms defined in RFC 9892 and RFC 9893, so the Security Considerations sections of those documents apply, as do the ones in RFC 8175.

The document names one inherited weakness: an injected message could resize a credit window to a value that results in a denial of service. The security mechanisms documented in RFC 8175 can be applied equally to the mechanism defined here.

It also warns about wildcards. Wildcards for matching the Priority Code Point (PCP) and VLAN Identifier (VID) fields, which come with the Ethernet-based credit window extension in RFC 9895, are convenient, because one rule can match a number of packet flows. They can also inadvertently match unexpected flows, or flows that appear only after the wildcard matching has been set up. The document therefore RECOMMENDS that wildcards not be used unless they are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who can inject DLEP messages could resize a credit window in a way that stops traffic, and the protections in the base DLEP document are the ones to use. The document also warns that a wildcard rule can match more traffic than you meant, including traffic that starts later, so it recommends using wildcards only when there is no alternative.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned one code point in the Extension Type Values registry, in the Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP) Parameters registry group. Code point 6 is the Diffserv Aware Credit Window extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension is registered with IANA as number 6 in the registry of DLEP extension types, so peers can recognise it from the number alone.
